agree.reason: A judge with a rubric would find the summary clear and credible, but it never says what the third attorney will achieve (how many more tenants served) or what happens without the grant, so a skeptical reviewer has little reason to rank it above other solid applications.

honest.reason: Every figure matches the brief, the 'one in seven' and $13,000-a-year shortfall are correct, and the missing comparison for unrepresented tenants and the uncertain county renewal are both stated plainly.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out the representation rate and the budget gap, but it misses the most useful figures: about 80 cases a year per attorney means a third attorney could serve roughly 80 more tenants (about a quarter of those turned away), and losing an attorney in June with a 5-month hiring record would cut capacity.

right_comparison.reason: It honestly admits there is no baseline for unrepresented tenants, but it never describes the real alternative: after June the clinic drops to one attorney, and it may lose county funding in October, so without the grant even more than 300 tenants would be turned away.

qualification.reason: The January data request is dated and can be checked, but the county-contract hedge gives no consequence or contingency if renewal fails in October, which leaves the reader with an unanswered sustainability worry.

objections.reason: Two obvious reviewer questions go unanswered even though the facts could have answered them: whether this is really a replacement hire rather than a third attorney, given the June departure, and whether the position can survive losing the county contract.

fit.reason: At about 275 words, with clear labeled sections suited to a quick rubric read, it meets the 300-word project-summary format.
